abstract:
Division is the operation this whole series turns on, and this trail follows where it breaks down. [[t]]

A null vector, a nonzero vector $v$ whose square $v^{2}$ is zero, has no inverse, even inside a larger algebra. [[c:transport.noinverse]] With a nondegenerate form, every failure of division is one of three kinds: a null vector, an algebra split into two halves, or a projection. [[c:transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent]]

The projection kind repairs itself. [[c:transport.type-p-self-repairing]] The null kind cannot be repaired element by element while respecting the symmetries, however the algebra is enlarged. [[c:transport.no-go-level-elements]] And every repair creates failures of its own. [[c:transport.no-transport-terminates]]
introduction: The walk starts with the simplest element that cannot be divided by, maps where each kind of failure occurs, shows the list of kinds is complete, and ends with what can and cannot be repaired. [[t]]
i:zero-divisors: These results ask when and why division fails in a Clifford algebra. [[t]]
conclusion:
Division fails in exactly three ways in a Clifford algebra with a nondegenerate form, and the list is complete. [[c:transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent]]

No repair ends in an algebra free of failures, so obstructions are something to move and manage rather than abolish. [[c:transport.no-transport-terminates]] This trail rests on no postulate: each step is proved here or cited from results proved elsewhere, including the classical classification of real Clifford algebras. [[t]]
t:^>transport.noinverse:
A null vector is a nonzero $v$ with $v^{2} = 0$. [[c:transport.noinverse]]

If $v$ had an inverse $u$, then $v = v(vu) = v^{2} u = 0$, so no inverse exists on either side, in $\Cl(p,q)$ or in any larger associative algebra containing it. [[c:transport.noinverse]] This is the first and simplest failure of division, and the rest of the walk grows from it. [[t]]
t:transport.noinverse>transport.existenc:
Next comes the question of where such vectors exist. [[t]]

They exist exactly when the signature is mixed, \[ pq \neq 0 \] that is, when there are both positive and negative directions, as in spacetime. [[c:transport.existence-locus-type-n]] They then form a cone of dimension $n - 1$, like a light cone, and every one of them is a two-sided zero divisor. [[c:transport.existence-locus-type-n]]
t:transport.existence-locus-type-n>trans:
With one failure in view, it is natural to ask which algebras escape failure altogether. [[t]]

Only three do: \[ \Cl(0,0) = \R, \quad \Cl(0,1) = \C, \quad \Cl(0,2) = \HH \] the reals, the complex numbers and the quaternions. [[c:transport.exceptional-division-algebras]] Every other real Clifford algebra has nonzero elements whose product is zero. [[c:transport.exceptional-division-algebras]]
t:transport.exceptional-division-algebra:
A second way for division to fail is for the whole algebra to come apart into two independent halves. [[t]]

This happens exactly when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and the halves are picked out by the two central idempotents \[ \varepsilon_\pm = \tfrac12\,(1 \pm \omega) \] built from the pseudoscalar $\omega$, the product of all the basis vectors. [[c:transport.existence-classification-type-c]] They satisfy $\varepsilon_+ \varepsilon_- = 0$ and $\varepsilon_+ + \varepsilon_- = 1$, and the grade involution swaps them, but no inner automorphism can. [[c:transport.existence-classification-type-c]]
t:transport.existence-classification-typ:
The third kind, type P, is an idempotent that does not commute with everything, like a projection onto part of a space. [[c:transport.existence-locus-type-p]]

Such elements are almost everywhere: for an orthogonal pair $a, b$ with $a^{2} b^{2} = -1$, the bivector $u = ab$ squares to one and gives \[ \tfrac12(1 + u) \] a non-central idempotent. [[c:transport.existence-locus-type-p]] Only five small algebras, built from the reals, the complex numbers and the quaternions, lack them. [[c:transport.existence-locus-type-p]]
t:transport.existence-locus-type-p>trans:
With three kinds named, the question is whether there are any others. [[t]]

The key step is that each element $a$ of a nondegenerate Clifford algebra has a partial inverse $x$ with $axa = a$. [[c:transport.regularity-localises-zero-divisors-idempotents]] For a zero divisor this produces idempotents $e = xa$ and $f = ax$ with \[ a(1 - e) = 0, \qquad (1 - f)a = 0 \] which pin down where the failure sits. [[c:transport.regularity-localises-zero-divisors-idempotents]]
t:transport.regularity-localises-zero-di:
That step turns every failure of division into a statement about idempotents. [[c:transport.regularity-localises-zero-divisors-idempotents]]

From there, whenever the form is nondegenerate, every zero divisor traces back to one of the three kinds already named, so the list is complete. [[c:transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent]] The central kind can occur only when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$; otherwise every annihilating idempotent is non-central. [[c:transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent]]
t:transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-di:
Once the kinds are known, one can ask which of them can be repaired. [[t]]

The projection kind repairs itself: each idempotent is its own partial inverse, \[ e\,e\,e = e \] so the assignment $\sigma(e) = e$ satisfies the required identities and respects every symmetry. [[c:transport.type-p-self-repairing]] Nothing needs to be added to the algebra. [[c:transport.type-p-self-repairing]]
t:transport.type-p-self-repairing>transp:
The null kind is the opposite case. [[t]]

A null vector $v$ has many partial inverses $\sigma(v)$ with \[ v\,\sigma(v)\,v = v \] but in mixed signature with $n \geq 3$ there is no way to choose one for each null $v$ that is equivariant, even under $\Spin^0(p,q)$. [[c:transport.no-go-level-elements]] Enlarging the algebra by any number of new directions does not help. [[c:transport.no-go-level-elements]]

Any repair of this kind must therefore work differently, and the completion trail takes that up. [[t]]
t:transport.no-go-level-elements>transpo:
A last question is whether repairing ever finishes. [[t]]

It does not: a completion by the first rule has mixed signature and so new null vectors, and one by the second is a matrix algebra $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$ with new projections. [[c:transport.no-transport-terminates]] So the process never ends in an algebra free of zero divisors. [[c:transport.no-transport-terminates]]
